To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the motor system is activated by affordances, which can be distinguished from spatial compatibility effects.

1) graspable objects facilitate motor responses, 2) this effect is independent from a spatial compatibility effect, 3) the facilitation is present only in the earliest stages of the motor system, 4) it is present in amputees, and 5) it is present for both arm and finger movements.
the presence of a handle on a centrally located object facilitates motor responses that match the handle position, but only at early stages of motor preparation and execution.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how we interact with objects and our environment in general.
the role of object affordances in action preparation, and how these affordances are represented in the brain.
the question how the human motor system interacts with the visual world and how this interaction is influenced by object properties and task requirements.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the visual perception of affordance of an object does not directly evoke an action, rather it prompts the motor system to be in a state ready to act.
affordances and spatial compatibilities effects are not the same, but they do share some commonalities.
the affordance effects in perception are not a mere by-product of spatial compatibility effects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
affordances do not automatically trigger the most appropriate action.

spatial compatibility effects are present at the early stages of action preparation, and affordance effects are present at later stages of action execution, suggesting that affordances are not necessarily evoked during action preparation.
spatial compatibility is a more fundamental effect than affordance, as affordance can be explained by a spatial compatibility effect.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the visual system does not only encode object properties, but also the possibilities for interaction with these objects, which may be useful for the design of more natural and intuitive human-robot interaction systems.

the visual features that are associated with an object's affordance can be used to facilitate motor responses, even when these responses are not necessarily associated with the object's affordance, and that the facilitation occurs in a body-part independent manner.
the visual system does not automatically select the most suitable action for the current situation, but instead provides a general motor signal that may be further processed by the motor system.
